cells.tense: You're here, with your eyes open, and what you're looking at is arriving without you forcing it.
cells.ask: Before you sleep tonight, write one line about the pull you're moving toward — just the line, no next move attached.
cells.core:
The pull you're following has shape tonight. You can feel which way is actually yours — the one that lands without argument — and you're moving by it without needing to prove the moving to anyone. Not performing the shine. Just walking where it points, and the walking itself is quiet.

That kind of clear look before the show is the early kind, not the finished kind. It doesn't have results yet, only a direction. So there's room to feed it: one line about what you're pulled toward, written down before you decide what to do next. What this leaves you is a place to come back to — the direction, sitting on paper where it can't drift.
cells.sheetLine: You can see which way is yours, and you're already walking it.
cells.verb: taking the first clean look at what's actually here
cells.place: in the pull toward what's light, before the shape of it shows

cells.tense: Ahead of you there's a version of this where the pull has already arrived, and you're bracing to meet it before it's here.
cells.ask: Do the smallest real thing you'd do if the direction were confirmed — one move, today — and leave the outcome completely unwatched.
cells.core:
This pull is live and your eyes are good, and the trouble is you're already living in the morning after the answer. You check whether the direction is real by doing one more thing first — one more proof, one more minute of reading the signs — and the checking has taken the place where the moving used to be. The moving hasn't stopped. It's just gone into overdrive about getting there.

On a normal day this pull shows up as an easy order — a few things matter and you go do them because you can tell which. That's what the good eyes are for: knowing which way to lean, so your hands can do a small real thing now. A step on the route, no result asked of it, gives the bracing its own rest. The route you get back belongs to the day you're in, not a day you've built in advance.
cells.sheetLine: You're checking the pull so hard the pull stopped moving you.

cells.tense: You're standing at a point where the direction was once set, and your eyes are there while the pull is happening today, right here.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you know is yours and finish a small piece of it today — something a camera could see, with an end.
cells.core:
The draw toward something real is still in you; it's just not moving you. When direction shows up it feels like it was settled before and there's nothing to point at now, so the whole subject stays in the drawer. The pull went quiet, not away. On a working day this pulls you forward without effort — you can feel which thing matters and you're already reaching for it.

Direction doesn't come back by feeling more ambitious. It comes back when a chosen piece of work is actually completed — a small thing with a beginning and an end, done on purpose, not because you suddenly wanted it. Finish one piece today and clear looking gets something real to stand on. What you're left with is your own grip on the direction; it reads on your hands before it reads as a feeling.
cells.sheetLine: The pull is still in you. It's stopped moving you.

cells.tense: You're already following something — the shape of your days points one way — and if asked you'd probably call it just getting through, not a direction.
cells.ask: Write one line on paper that finishes this sentence: the direction this life keeps moving in is ___, and sign it — as if it wrote itself.
cells.core:
There's a current that keeps showing up in what you do — the choice that repeats, the thing that won't stop catching your eye — and you haven't been billing it as the direction. You call it circumstance, or the momentum of the week. The pull is running under a name that isn't its own, and because it's been renamed it doesn't get steered by anyone. On a good day this would look like glancing up and re-aiming without fuss — the way you'd correct a route you already know.

Underneath all the renaming there's a first clear look that came early. Put it in a sentence of your own, and sign it. What you're signing for is the re-aiming that was already possible; once the direction is out in your handwriting, the steering has a hand on it again.
